summary:
Mission ARES is a browser game for kids aged 7–12 in which they run a small Mars outpost for two sols. Every choice trades three shared resources, Power, Water and Air: water the greenhouse or save it for the shield, heat the rover or risk the cold, wait for advice from Earth or go now.

Real NASA data drives the rules, not just the facts on screen. A live solar storm from NASA DONKI (with the WSA-Enlil model) sets the storm forecast, and the forecast can be wrong, so building a thicker water shield is a real gamble. Today's Earth–Mars message delay, worked out from NASA/JPL planet positions, decides how long players wait for help. Real Curiosity radiation readings from NASA RadLab and a space-plant study from NASA OSDR show what happened on Mars.

Kids learn that in space, and on Earth, nothing is free: every resource you use is one you can't use for something else. The game ends by linking each lesson to life on Earth, from water recycling to desert farming in Egypt.
details:
## What it does

Mission ARES is a story-driven resource-management game for kids aged 7–12 (ages 9–12 can play alone; younger players with a parent or teacher). The player is a boy who joins a crew landing at Jezero Crater on Mars. Over two Martian days the crew must keep three shared resources, Power, Water and Air, alive while doing their mission work:

- Greenhouse: choose how much water and light to give a real space crop (radish, lettuce, chile pepper...). More water means more food, but less water for later.

- Garage and rover: pick a heater for today's real Mars temperature, wait for advice from Earth or leave now, and drive to collect the rock scientists asked for.

- Night: solve an oxygen puzzle as the base runs on batteries until sunrise.

- Solar storm: a real solar eruption heads for Mars. Mission Control sends a forecast, and the player picks a thin, medium or thick water shield. Thicker is safer but costs more Power and locks up Water.

At the end, players get a score, see every choice they made and its effect, and read "Back on Earth" cards that connect each lesson to real life.

## How NASA data drives the game

- NASA DONKI (CME, with WSA-Enlil runs): the game fetches a real coronal mass ejection from the last 30 days that NASA's model sends toward Mars. Its speed and proton events set the storm forecast and the arrival date. If NASA can't be reached, one of three saved real events is used. The DONKI event ID is shown on screen.

- NASA/JPL planet positions: today's Earth–Mars radio delay is calculated live. It sets how long the rover waits for Earth's reply, and explains why a big flare's particles arrive before any forecast can.

- NASA RadLab (OSDR): real hourly radiation readings from Curiosity's RAD in May 2024 are drawn as a chart, flat at about 4 µGy/h, then 304 µGy/h when a storm hit Mars (about 74× higher).

- NASA OSDR (OSD-268): a real study of plants grown in space is shown in the greenhouse.

- Perseverance MEDA weather, NASA/JPL Photojournal images of Jezero's delta and of a solar eruption, and NASA Earth Observatory images of Egypt's farmland support the scenes.

Every fact on screen shows its source, and a "NASA data" screen lists them all, including a separate list of numbers we made up for game balance.

## Why it matters (impact)

The challenge asks kids to understand trade-offs: in a closed habitat, every resource you use is one you can't use for something else. That is also true on Earth. In Egypt, only about 4% of the land can grow crops and almost all water comes from the Nile. Water recycling, growing food with little water, and preparing for space weather that can hit satellites and power grids are real Earth problems. The game ends by linking each Mars decision to one of them, so kids carry the lesson home.

## What makes it creative

- Live data is part of the rules, not just shown: the real forecast can be wrong, so kids learn to plan for uncertainty, the way real mission planners do.

- The real Earth–Mars message delay turns "waiting for help" into a decision.

- Kids see real Mars data (a radiation chart, a real eruption photo, a real delta photo), not just numbers in text.

- All the art, animation and sound are made in code: no image or sound files besides two real NASA photos.

## Design choices we considered

- Three resources only (Power, Water, Air) plus crew mood, as the challenge suggests, so kids can track everything on one tablet screen.

- No choice is free and no choice is always right. We wrote a balance checker that played every possible choice combination (540 situations, 1.86 million games) to make sure of this, and set the badge scores from the results.

- Short sentences and a pause button for young readers, plus story speed controls.

- Works offline or when NASA's servers are slow: every live call has a saved real fallback.

- Judge Mode and a "For judges" panel make the demo repeatable and jump straight to the key moments.

- Honesty: a "Made up for the game" list separates game rules from real NASA data.

## Tools and technologies

React, TypeScript and Vite; SVG for all graphics; the Web Audio API for sound; NASA Open APIs (DONKI); NASA OSDR RadLab data API; Node's built-in test runner (automated tests) and oxlint. Runs in any modern browser, on a laptop or a tablet.

## Team

Fares Mostafa, Merna Hossam, Eman Ahmed, Amr Obaia, Ahmed Zahran (Team Alienated, NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026).

## Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write and review code and text. No AI-generated images, video or audio are in the game. All facts are checked against the NASA sources listed in the game.
